documents.title: AI 101 - Campus Edition
documents.summary: An OTL explainer that says UCSB has no formal AI policy as of Summer 2025 and helps instructors build their own through scenarios, sample policies and discussion questions. It quotes the Student Conduct rule, offers prompts for instructors and students, and notes data privacy.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'neither UCSB nor the UC system has a formal policy' and gives instructors scenarios, sample policies and prompts so each decides course by course, and it quotes Student Conduct's rule that unapproved AI is dishonesty. Because the page itself sets no stance and hands decisions to instructors, it is coded delegates.

units.why: Defines generative AI via a quoted source ('Subset of AI that focuses on creating new data or content'). Definition that scopes the topic: P61.
units.anchor: Subset of AI that focuses on creating new data or content

units.why: Says the goal is 'to help you navigate how to use, or not use, AI'; the series (AI 102 on literacy, AI 103 on critical thinking) is AI-literacy education for instructors and students: P70.
units.anchor: AI 102 covers the Fundamentals of AI Literacy.
units.fit_note: Describes a series of OTL pages rather than a mandated training.

units.why: UCUES statistics (e.g., 25% use AI for coding; over 85% find professors' policies reasonable) are evidence on student use and views, so P55.
units.anchor: Of 6277 survey respondents:
units.fit_note: Cites survey data on usage and perception, not learning outcomes.

units.why: States 'neither UCSB nor the UC system has a formal policy on generative AI in teaching and learning contexts' and that policy-making is complicated because the field evolves. It leaves the choice to instructors, so P04, partial fit.
units.anchor: neither UCSB nor the UC system has a formal policy on generative AI
units.fit_note: Says no formal institutional policy exists; the delegation to instructors is implied by the surrounding advice.

units.why: Because 'creating policies around AI use are complicated because it is rapidly evolving', policy is provisional; frames change over time: P54.
units.anchor: creating policies around AI use are complicated because it is rapidly evolving
units.fit_note: Notes evolution as difficulty; no commitment to revisit.

units.why: Tells instructors to 'consider what you would do if the following scenarios occurred in your course' (translation, summaries, coding help, uploading slides). Instructors decide per scenario: P04.
units.anchor: consider what you would do if the following scenarios occurred in your course

units.why: 'meet with an Instructional Consultant at OTL for feedback on your policy' is faculty support: P63.
units.anchor: meet with an Instructional Consultant at OTL for feedback on your policy

units.why: OTL 'has compiled sample Generative AI policies that you can adapt for your course'. Provides templates and advice for instructors: P63.
units.anchor: sample Generative AI policies that you can adapt for your course and assignments
units.fit_note: Sample policy language rather than workshops.

units.why: Quotes Student Conduct standards that academic dishonesty includes 'utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from the instructor' and 'Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs'. Misconduct classification: P36.
units.anchor: utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from the instructor

units.why: Quotes the Writing Program: 'Communicate clear guidelines and expectations regarding the use of AI writing technology in the classroom'. Instructors state expectations: P09.
units.anchor: Communicate clear guidelines and expectations regarding the use of AI writing technology in the classroom

units.why: The same quote requires 'proper, clear, and continual attribution of any use of AI writing tools'. Disclosure rule: P24.
units.anchor: the need for proper, clear, and continual attribution of any use of AI writing tools

units.why: 'it is very important that you talk about your Gen AI policies in class and with your teaching assistants' asks instructors to discuss rules with students and TAs: P66.
units.anchor: it is very important that you talk about your Gen AI policies in class

units.why: 'consider making some common ground rules with students about what is and isn't acceptable' means setting expectations jointly: P67.
units.anchor: making some common ground rules with students about what is and isn't acceptable

units.why: Poses questions such as 'What is AI good for in this class?' and 'Why might we choose not to use it' to start student conversations: P66.
units.anchor: What is AI good for in this class?

units.why: Asks instructors to settle with TAs 'Do you have any stipulations about the TA using AI for tasks related to their role as TA?'. TA/instructor AI use for teaching tasks: P59.
units.anchor: stipulations about the TA using AI for tasks related to their role as TA

units.why: 'There are many ethical ways that you can use AI to improve your own efficiency and effectiveness as a teacher' with course preparation, encouraging instructors: P59.
units.anchor: There are many ethical ways that you can use AI to improve your own efficiency

units.why: Rubric Generator prompt: 'give the AI your assignment instructions, and let it create a rubric'. Instructor use of AI to draft a rubric: P59.
units.anchor: give the AI your assignment instructions, and let it create a rubric for you.

units.why: Points to 'prompt engineering basics for teachers' for prompting advice: P93.
units.anchor: prompt engineering basics for teachers

units.why: Tells students whose instructor has not addressed AI that 'you should talk to the instructor or TA' about which uses help. Ask when unsure: P10.
units.anchor: you should talk to the instructor or TA about which of these ideas

units.why: 'Socratic Tutor - let the AI tutor you with a series of questions that adapt to your understanding' is a study-use tutoring suggestion for students: P12.
units.anchor: let the AI tutor you with a series of questions that adapt to your understanding

units.why: Copy Editor: 'it doesn't write from scratch for you, but it will give you feedback on things like style, clarity and flow'. Editing support: P91.
units.anchor: it doesn't write from scratch for you, but it will give you feedback

units.why: Innovation Incubator 'helps you bring your creative ideas to life as it guides you in creating a plan for your projects'. Brainstorming support: P15.
units.anchor: helps you bring your creative ideas to life

units.why: Warns that platforms 'use the content that we put into them to train the models' and shows how to opt out. Data privacy: P50.
units.anchor: they also use the content that we put into them to train the models

documents.title: Academic Integrity (Student Conduct)
documents.summary: The Office of Student Conduct page lists unapproved or unauthorized AI use as plagiarism within its definition of academic dishonesty. It is brief, with two AI lines and no guidance on permitted use.
documents.stance_why: The page lists 'utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from instructor' as plagiarism and 'Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs to complete course work' as dishonesty, so AI is banned unless approved: restrict. It sets no tiers and does not simply hand the choice to instructors.

units.why: States that any submission for an academic requirement 'must represent a student's original work', a general ownership rule that the page applies to AI below. Assigned P29 because it requires submitted work to be the student's own; no AI-specific type fits better.
units.anchor: must represent a student's original work

units.why: Lists 'utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from instructor' under Plagiarism, so unapproved AI use is classed as misconduct. P36 fits (classification as plagiarism); P06 does not since this is a misconduct definition, not a syllabus-silence fallback, though approval is implied as the default requirement.
units.anchor: utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from instructor
units.policy: Utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from the instructor is plagiarism.

units.why: A separate bullet says 'Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs to complete course work' is academic dishonesty. Classified P36 as it names unauthorized AI use as a misconduct category; it is a distinct listing (about completing coursework) rather than approval-for-credit.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs to complete course work

units.why: Cheating category bans 'unauthorized material such as notes, cheat sheets, or electronic devices during an exam'. Not AI-named, but it governs devices (which would include AI tools) on exams, so P22 is the nearest type; fit is partial because AI is not mentioned.
units.anchor: Using any unauthorized material such as notes, cheat sheets, or electronic devices during an exam
units.fit_note: Does not mention AI; covers unauthorized electronic devices on exams generally.

documents.unit: Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost / OTL
documents.title: Guidance Regarding AI-Writing Assistance Technologies
documents.summary: A 2023 memo from the Office of Teaching and Learning, sent via the provost's office, states that AI writing assistance is disallowed unless an instructor allows it, advises against AI detectors, and offers ideas for scaffolding and incorporating AI. It names coding in scope but its guidance is framed around writing.
documents.stance_why: The memo says student AI writing use 'is not allowed in courses ... unless specifically allowed by the instructor or supervisor', a default ban with instructor permission, while also urging instructors to consider incorporating AI. No tiers are offered. Coded restrict because the stated default is not allowed unless permitted.

units.why: The memo says it gives 'guidance about the ethical use' of AI-assistive technologies by instructors and students, including 'writing, coding, drawing, and completing equations'. This defines the scope, including coding, so P61 (define AI and scope) fits.
units.anchor: writing, coding, drawing, and completing equations

units.why: Heading 1 tells instructors to 'Communicate expectations for student use' of AI in courses and other documents. It is addressed to instructors and is advice (should), so P09 fits.
units.anchor: Communicate expectations for student use of AI-writing assistive technologies in courses

units.why: States that AI writing use 'falls within the purview of the Student Conduct Code'. It classifies AI misuse under the integrity code, so P36 over P77 (which is about general legal compliance).
units.anchor: falls within the purview of the Student Conduct Code

units.why: 'student use of AI-assistive technology for writing is not allowed ... unless specifically allowed by the instructor' sets a default ban with instructor permission as the exception. P06 (fallback rule) chosen over P01 because the emphasis is what applies absent instructor permission.
units.anchor: student use of AI-assistive technology for writing is not allowed in courses
units.policy: Student use of AI-assistive technology for writing is not allowed in courses unless specifically allowed by the instructor or supervisor.
units.fit_note: Default ban stated for writing in courses; not tied to a silent syllabus explicitly.

units.why: The same sentence extends the ban to 'theses, dissertations, research articles' unless the supervisor allows. This is a research-scholarship rule, so P62; the course default is coded separately.
units.anchor: on theses, dissertations, research articles, etc. unless specifically allowed by the instructor or supervisor
units.policy: Student use of AI-assistive technology for writing is not allowed on theses, dissertations, research articles, etc. unless specifically allowed by the supervisor.

units.why: 'Explain "why."' tells instructors to give reasons for how AI should or should not be used. It goes beyond listing the rule, so P66.
units.anchor: increasingly important for instructors to explain why and how AI tools should/should not be used

units.why: Lists considerations to explain: 'developing students' critical thoughts/voice/skills'. It gives the learning rationale for limiting AI, so P41.
units.anchor: developing students' critical thoughts/voice/skills
units.policy: Considerations in explaining AI rules include developing students' critical thoughts/voice/skills.

units.why: Suggests instructors 'Consider including a policy statement specifically about the use of AI tools' with sample syllabus language. Advice to put AI expectations in the syllabus: P09.
units.anchor: Consider including a policy statement specifically about the use of AI tools

units.why: 'UCSB does not support the use of plagiarism detection software (e.g. Turnitin, ChatGPT Zero)' is an institutional stance against detectors, so P39.
units.anchor: UCSB does not support the use of plagiarism detection software

units.why: Gives the reason that 'Anti-plagiarism software is highly fallible' and detection is 'always one step behind'. Reliability reasons for not using detectors: P39.
units.anchor: Anti-plagiarism software is highly fallible.

units.why: Warns that submitting student work to detectors 'may violate students' intellectual property rights' because the student 'may lose ownership'. Ownership of inputs, so P52 (P50 privacy fits less since the concern is ownership).
units.anchor: Submitting student work to anti-plagiarism software may violate students' intellectual property rights.

units.why: Says detector use 'can undermine the fundamental relationship of trust' between learners and teachers. A further reason against detectors: P39.
units.anchor: Use of anti-plagiarism software can undermine the fundamental relationship of trust

units.why: Advises moving 'from detection to prevention' by crafting 'assignments and activities that cannot be produced by LLMs'. Assignment redesign: P35.
units.anchor: craft assignments and activities that cannot be produced by LLMs

units.why: OTL 'instructional consultants offer extensive support' to instructors changing their approach. Faculty support: P63.
units.anchor: instructional consultants offer extensive support for instructors

units.why: 'Instructors and TAs should not use AI-assistive technology for grading and feedback unless the technology is supported by UCSB' allows it only for vetted, contracted tools (Gradescope). Conditions on AI grading: P101 rather than P46 since it does not say only humans grade.
units.anchor: Instructors and TAs should not use AI-assistive technology for grading and feedback unless
units.policy: Instructors and TAs should not use AI-assistive technology for grading and feedback unless the technology is supported by UCSB.

units.why: 'If you suspect unauthorized use of AI technologies, submit an incident report' tells instructors to file with the Office of Student Conduct. Formal reporting step: P81.
units.anchor: If you suspect unauthorized use of AI technologies, submit an

units.why: Asks the reporter to 'include any samples of earlier/baseline student writing' for comparison. Names a kind of evidence to weigh: P69.
units.anchor: include any samples of earlier/baseline student writing

units.why: 'Scaffold writing assignments' with smaller pieces and feedback is a design response to avoid AI problems: P35.
units.anchor: Scaffold writing assignments, so that students are writing smaller pieces

units.why: 'Add brief reflective writing' asking students to analyze their choices is an assignment design tactic by instructors, so P35; P26 is about students keeping logs of AI use, which this does not require.
units.anchor: Add brief reflective writing to assignments

units.why: 'Talk with students about the purpose of writing in the course and work with students to use LLMs in productive ways' asks instructors to discuss with students: P66.
units.anchor: Talk with students about the purpose of writing in the course

units.why: 'Assign topics that require personal reflection or creative thinking' is an assignment redesign: P35.
units.anchor: Assign topics that require personal reflection or creative thinking.

units.why: 'Create assignments where students use LLMs as part of the writing/thinking activities' invites building AI into coursework: P79 (use built in), encouraging.
units.anchor: Create assignments where students use LLMs as part of the writing/thinking activities.

units.why: Suggests discussions of 'writing processes, strategies, and ethics' using AI writing technology and examining strengths and weaknesses with students. Class discussion about AI: P66.
units.anchor: Stimulate discussions about writing processes, strategies, and ethics through discussions of AI writing technology.

units.why: 'leveraging AI writing technology to create prompts, topics, or questions for exploration' encourages brainstorming-type use: P15.
units.anchor: leveraging AI writing technology to create prompts, topics, or questions for exploration

units.why: 'Invite students to utilize AI to generate text in specific genres' to study genre conventions: AI built into coursework, P79.
units.anchor: Invite students to utilize AI to generate text in specific genres

units.why: 'compare AI-generated text with human-generated text' as a classroom activity: P79 (AI-use built into an activity).
units.anchor: Encourage students to compare AI-generated text with human-generated text

units.why: Notes LLMs 'hallucinate' and tells instructors to 'Urge students to cross-check AI-generated information'. Verification of output: P31.
units.anchor: Urge students to cross-check AI-generated information and develop critical appraisal skills

units.why: Asks instructors to 'Examine and address potential biases and fairness concerns' such as stereotypes. Bias concerns: P53.
units.anchor: Examine and address potential biases and fairness concerns that may arise from AI writing technology

units.why: 'Think about your course objectives. What are the cognitive tasks students need to perform without AI assistance?' ties AI decisions to learning objectives: P83.
units.anchor: Think about your course objectives.

notes: Scenario questions in the OTL page and external resource lists were not coded as policies. The EVC memo (2023) may be partly superseded by the OTL AI 101 page (2025). Several OTL units use P63/P66/P04 with fit notes.
